title: Litmus: Fair Pricing for Serverless Computing
problem: Serverless platforms charge tenants based on function execution time, but when multiple functions run concurrently, system congestion causes performance degradation. Tenants incur higher costs during slowdowns caused by co-location contention, despite having no control over system-wide resource availability.
motivation: Current serverless pricing models are fundamentally unfair because they penalize tenants for performance degradation caused by system overload rather than their own resource inefficiency.
method: Litmus watches how long your function takes to run and compares it to how long it would take if the server was empty. The difference is slowdown from other functions using the same CPU and memory. Litmus charges you for the empty-server time instead of the actual time, removing the penalty for system congestion you didn't cause.
key_novelty: Litmus charges you for the execution time your function would have used on an empty server, not the actual time it took with other functions present.
contributions: Identifies and formalizes the unfair pricing problem in serverless computing when functions suffer co-location slowdowns
Proposes Litmus, a fair pricing mechanism that accounts for system congestion in billing
Provides framework for analyzing cost-performance fairness under function multiplexing
Decouples tenant billing from system-wide resource contention effects
limitations: Limitations regarding deployment overhead, scalability to large clusters, or assumptions about contention detection are not discussed in the provided abstract.
primary_theme: fair billing for serverless functions under system contention
